reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes participation in a BNB pool advertising 10% daily returns and 3650% APR, while explicitly acknowledging that the scheme has no real mining and requires new investors to pay earlier participants. Despite those warnings, the speaker says viewers may get returns by joining the first wave, demonstrates investing in the project, offers a referral link, and concludes that viewers can give the miner a try.

citations.quote: So if you are on the first wave, you may get your return within a month, and anything from then onward is just pure profit
This is the Ponzi scheme. There's no real miner going on here.
I will have a refferre link for this project
you can give this Pisa Miner a try

opening.argument: The video repeatedly makes the downside explicit rather than assuring viewers of safe or guaranteed profit: the speaker says the advertised return is not paid in BNB, depends on new investors, and could be worthless. He labels the arrangement a Ponzi scheme, warns viewers not to expect to retire from it, and tells them to do their own due diligence. The description likewise says he will not recommend the project at this stage. A viewer can read the invitation to assess the project in light of those unusually direct warnings, not as a concealed promise.

citations.quote: The 10% Daily is only achievable if you compound 60% and withdraw 1 day. And if there's no new investors coming in, you'll not get your 10%.
This is the Ponzi scheme. There's no real miner going on here.
Do not think that by investing in this you can quit your job and retire
I'm not a financial advisor, so you have to do your own due diligence and decide if you want to go in or not
I wont be recommending this project

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening emphasizes the most promotional excerpts but does not erase the video's qualifications. The speaker explains that the stated return is conditional, not a BNB payout, and warns that without new investors it will not materialize. His personal participation does not establish that he represents the pool as safe or guaranteed; he directly calls it a Ponzi scheme and cautions viewers against relying on it for retirement.

citations.quote: The 10% Daily is only achievable if you compound 60% and withdraw 1 day.
This is the Ponzi scheme. There's no real miner going on here.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The warnings are candid, but they sit alongside a clear invitation to participate: the speaker says early entrants may get their return, demonstrates his own investment, plans to invest more, and concludes that viewers can give it a try. Calling the pool a Ponzi scheme does not neutralize the promotion when he also explains how to seek an early payout.

opening.argument: Much of the video is framed as a practical explanation of how to evaluate a DeFi project: checking for an audit, watching membership trends, considering timing, and comparing BNB input with output. The speaker also walks through how to distinguish the project site from a fake one and what wallet permissions to inspect. He says the available input/output data is limited because the project had only just launched. That is educational commentary and a personal demonstration, not evidence that the video establishes the project's claims as reliable.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening treats the tutorial elements as a route to a scam rather than asking what the video actually demonstrates. The speaker highlights auditing, warns about impersonation sites and discusses wallet permissions; these are concrete evaluation and security topics. He also admits there is not yet enough contract-flow data, which is inconsistent with presenting the investment as verified or settled.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The evaluation advice is not the video's only function. The speaker moves from explaining checks to urging early entry, demonstrates his own purchase, discusses the return opportunity, and invites viewers to try it. A tutorial about wallet permissions cannot establish that the pool's promised returns are sound, particularly when he acknowledges dependence on new investors.

opening.argument: The video shows an ordinary project interface and a wallet-connection flow, but the supplied material does not show a completed transfer caused by authorization, a hidden credential request, or an actual payout. The speaker describes the displayed connection permission as limited to viewing the address and balance and suggesting transactions. He also distinguishes the genuine site from an impersonation site and directs viewers to verify the audit source. A project interface, referral feature, or wallet prompt alone does not prove deceptive theft or a completed scam mechanism.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening infers a completed deceptive mechanism that the cited evidence does not establish. The speaker explicitly warns against the fake site and explains the limited permission he says appeared; the frame shows a connection prompt, not proof of an unauthorized transfer. The discussion of a referral link likewise does not by itself establish that viewers were deceived or that a payment occurred.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The absence of a shown theft does not answer the investment-pool concern. The video advertises fixed daily returns and a referral reward, encourages early participation, and the speaker admits there is no real mining and new investors are needed for returns. The connection screen is not the core issue; the promotion of the pool is.
